paragraphs: Friend, here's the big idea. The psalmist doesn't treat God's word like a rulebook he puts up with. He says, "Oh, how I love Your law!" and calls it "sweeter than honey in my mouth!" (Psalm 119:97, 103). He says he has more insight than his teachers because God's testimonies are his meditation, and he discerns more than the elders because he obeys God's precepts (Psalm 119:99, 100).

Now look at verse 105, because I'd stamp this one on every cookie if the letters fit: "Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path." A lamp doesn't show you the whole road at once. It shows you where to put your foot next, and that's the kind of help we need on hard days. The psalmist is severely afflicted and says the wicked have set a snare for him, and he still says, "I do not forget Your law" and "I have not strayed from Your precepts" (Psalm 119:107, 109, 110). His hard days didn't push the word out, and his answer was to ask God to revive him through it.

So what do you do with this, baker? Do what he does: call the LORD your hiding place and your shield, and put your hope in His word (Psalm 119:114). He also ends honestly, saying his flesh trembles in awe of the LORD, so loving God's word and standing in awe of God go together (Psalm 119:120). Keep the oven warm, because Psalm 119 isn't finished yet.
